# Results
In this chapter, we present the main results of our analysis. First we showcase the prevalence of the beta anomaly by testing proposition 1 and then we present the performance of the BAB-portfolio to test proposition 2. Lastly, we present the results of our extension of proposition 2 by introducing transaction costs into our analysis.

## Proposition 1: The Security Market Line

To test proposition 1 we run Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of monthly excess returns on lagged betas. The results are presented below. The intercept is positive and highly statistically significant with a mean of 0.79% per month and a t-statistic of 5.89, indicating that there is a substantial return that is unrelated to market beta. More central to proposition 1, the slope coefficient on beta is 0.14% per month with a t-statistic of only 0.75, which is statistically indistinguishable from zero. Under the CAPM, this slope should equal the market excess return, which over our sample averages considerably higher. The near-zero and insignificant beta coefficient therefore indicates that the cross-sectional compensation for bearing systematic risk is far smaller than the CAPM predicts, consistent with a flatter-than-predicted security market line and with the beta anomaly. We note that the empirical SML plotted below appears to slope slightly downward, while the Fama-MacBeth coefficient is slightly positive. This apparent tension reflects different weighting: Fama-MacBeth weights all individual stocks equally within each month, so the moderate-beta stocks that constitute the bulk of the cross-section determine the average slope. The decile-based SML, by contrast, fits a line through ten equally-weighted group averages, giving the extreme high-beta decile (average beta ≈ 2.1) disproportionate leverage on the fitted slope. Both results are fully consistent with the beta anomaly and proposition 1: the empirical compensation for beta is economically negligible and statistically indistinguishable from zero, far below the CAPM prediction.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-fmb-results
#| tbl-cap: "Fama-MacBeth regression results. Time-series averages of monthly cross-sectional coefficients of excess returns on lagged beta. The mean is expressed in percent per month. $t$-statistics are computed from the time-series standard error of the monthly estimates. Sample: US equities, January 1963 to December 2025."
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| output: asis
fmb_display = pd.DataFrame({
    "Mean (\\%/month)": (fmb_summary["mean"] * 100).round(4),
    "$t$-statistic": fmb_summary["t_stat"].round(2)
})
fmb_display.index = ["Intercept", "Beta"]
print(tabulate(
    fmb_display,
    headers=["", "Mean (\\%/month)", "$t$-statistic"],
    tablefmt="latex_booktabs",
    floatfmt=".4f"
))
```

### Beta-Sorted Portfolio Alphas

The Fama-MacBeth results are complemented by an analysis of CAPM alphas across beta-sorted decile portfolios. Sorting all stocks into ten groups by their estimated beta and computing each decile's average monthly CAPM alpha reveals a striking monotone pattern. Low-beta deciles earn positive and statistically significant alphas: decile 1 (average beta of 0.49) earns 0.27% per month, while deciles 2 and 3 earn 0.22% and 0.25% per month, both significant at conventional levels with t-statistics above 2.4 and 3.2, respectively. Moving up the beta distribution, alphas decline steadily. Decile 6 is essentially zero (-0.01%, t=−0.20), and the three highest-beta deciles earn negative and increasingly significant alphas. Decile 9 (average beta 1.64) earns -0.46% per month (t=−2.63), and the top decile (average beta 2.10) earns -0.82% per month (t=−3.16). This monotone decline in alpha across the beta distribution is precisely what proposition 1 predicts. The two panels below visualise this result: the upper panel plots the empirical security market line (solid blue) against the CAPM prediction (red dashed), showing that the empirical line is clearly flatter; the lower panel displays the CAPM alpha for each decile, illustrating the transition from positive alphas at the low end to large negative alphas at the high end.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-decile-alphas
#| tbl-cap: "CAPM alpha by beta decile. Value-weighted CAPM alpha for each beta-decile portfolio, estimated from time-series regressions of portfolio excess returns on the market excess return. Deciles are formed monthly by sorting on lagged Vasicek-shrunk beta. Green shading indicates positive alpha; red shading indicates negative alpha. Sample: US equities, January 1963 to December 2025."
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| output: asis
max_abs = decile_alphas["alpha"].abs().max()

lines = [
    r"\begin{tabular}{rccr}",
    r"\toprule",
    r"Decile & Avg.\ $\hat{\beta}$ & Monthly $\alpha$ (\%) & $t$-statistic \\",
    r"\midrule",
]
for _, row in decile_alphas.sort_values("beta_decile").iterrows():
    alpha = row["alpha"]
    alpha_t = row["alpha_t"]
    avg_beta = row["avg_beta"]
    decile = int(row["beta_decile"])
    pct = min(int(80 * abs(alpha) / max_abs), 80) if max_abs > 0 else 0
    color = "green!" + str(pct) if alpha >= 0 else "red!" + str(pct)
    sign = "+" if alpha >= 0 else ""
    lines.append(
        "\\rowcolor{" + color + "} "
        + str(decile) + " & "
        + f"{avg_beta:.2f}" + " & "
        + sign + f"{alpha * 100:.2f}" + " & "
        + f"{alpha_t:.2f}" + " \\\\"
    )
lines += [r"\bottomrule", r"\end{tabular}"]
print("\n".join(lines))
```

## Proposition 2: The BAB Factor

Having established the presence of the beta anomaly, we now turn to proposition 2 and examine whether a BAB portfolio that exploits this anomaly generates positive excess returns. Following Frazzini and Pedersen (2014), we construct the BAB factor each month by going long a leveraged portfolio of below-median-beta stocks and short a de-leveraged portfolio of above-median-beta stocks, with both legs scaled to a beta of one. The performance statistics are reported below. The BAB factor earns an annualised mean return of 8.85% with an annualised standard deviation of 11.26%, yielding a Sharpe ratio of 0.79. The associated t-statistic of 6.08 indicates that the positive mean return is highly statistically significant, providing strong support for proposition 2. The cumulative return chart below illustrates the time-series behaviour of the strategy: starting from $1 in the early 1960s, the portfolio grows substantially through the 1990s, partially retraces during 2000–2010, before recovering and compounding further toward the end of the sample. The strategy thus generates meaningful returns over the full sample period, albeit with considerable variation across sub-periods.

Sample: US equities, January 1963 to December 2025."

```{python}
#| label: compute-bab-legs
#| cache: true
bab_valid = bab_returns.dropna(subset=["r_bab"])
avg_lev_long = (1 / bab_valid["beta_L"].abs()).mean()
avg_lev_short = (1 / bab_valid["beta_H"].abs()).mean()

bab_legs = (
    bab_valid
    .assign(
        cum_bab=lambda x: (1 + x["r_bab"]).cumprod(),
        cum_long=lambda x: (1 + x["r_L"] / x["beta_L"].abs()).cumprod(),
        cum_short=lambda x: (1 + -(x["r_H"] / x["beta_H"].abs())).cumprod(),
        date=lambda x: x["month"].astype("datetime64[ns]")
    )
)

bab_legs_melt = pd.melt(
    bab_legs[["date", "cum_bab", "cum_long", "cum_short"]],
    id_vars="date",
    value_vars=["cum_bab", "cum_long", "cum_short"],
    var_name="series",
    value_name="cum_ret"
).assign(
    series=lambda x: x["series"].map({
        "cum_bab": "BAB total",
        "cum_long": "Long leg",
        "cum_short": "Short leg"
    })
)
```

The strong cumulative returns in @fig-bab-cumret-results are achieved with embedded leverage. The long leg scales returns by $1/\beta^L$, and since the low-beta portfolio has $\beta^L < 1$, the long side invests on margin. Over our sample the average leverage multiple on the long leg is `{python} f"{avg_lev_long:.2f}"` — meaning every \$1 of BAB capital controls roughly \$`{python} f"{avg_lev_long:.2f}"` of low-beta exposure — while the short leg is de-levered to a scaling factor of `{python} f"{avg_lev_short:.2f}"`. The impressive compounding visible in the figure therefore partly reflects this structural leverage, and returns would be materially lower if the long leg were held unlevered.

@fig-bab-legs decomposes the cumulative return into its long and short leg contributions separately, clarifying which side drives performance and when.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bab-legs
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative return decomposition of the BAB factor by leg. The long leg compounds $(1 + r^L_e/\\beta^L)$ and the short leg compounds $(1 - r^H_e/\\beta^H)$, each starting from \\$1. A rising short leg indicates the de-levered short position in high-beta stocks contributed positively. The BAB total combines both. Sample: US equities, January 1963 to December 2025."
(
    ggplot(bab_legs_melt, aes(x="date", y="cum_ret", color="series", linetype="series"))
    + geom_line(size=0.8)
    + scale_x_datetime(date_breaks="10 years", date_labels="%Y")
    + scale_y_log10()
    + scale_color_manual(values={
        "BAB total": "steelblue",
        "Long leg": "#2ca02c",
        "Short leg": "#d62728"
    })
    + scale_linetype_manual(values={
        "BAB total": "solid",
        "Long leg": "dashed",
        "Short leg": "dotted"
    })
    + labs(x="Date", y="Cumulative Return (\\$1 Invested, log scale)", color="", linetype="")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(legend_position="bottom")
)
```

@tbl-bab-subperiod decomposes BAB performance across four sub-periods to examine when the strategy performs and when it falters. The periods reflect structural transitions in the data: the pre-1990 early period; the strong 1990s bull market; the 2001–2009 decade encompassing the dot-com crash and the global financial crisis; and the post-crisis period from 2010 onward.

```{python}
#| label: compute-bab-subperiod
#| cache: true
def subperiod_stats(r, label):
    r = r.dropna()
    n = len(r)
    ann_mean = r.mean() * 12
    ann_std = r.std() * np.sqrt(12)
    sharpe = ann_mean / ann_std if ann_std > 0 else np.nan
    t = r.mean() / (r.std() / np.sqrt(n)) if n > 1 else np.nan
    return pd.Series({"Period": label, "Ann. Mean": ann_mean,
                      "Ann. Std": ann_std, "Sharpe": sharpe,
                      "t-stat": t, "N": int(n)})

bab_ts = bab_returns.dropna(subset=["r_bab"]).copy()
bab_ts["year"] = pd.DatetimeIndex(bab_ts["month"]).year

period_masks = [
    (bab_ts["year"] < 1990, "1963--1989"),
    ((bab_ts["year"] >= 1990) & (bab_ts["year"] < 2001), "1990--2000"),
    ((bab_ts["year"] >= 2001) & (bab_ts["year"] < 2010), "2001--2009"),
    (bab_ts["year"] >= 2010, "2010--2025"),
]

subperiod_df = pd.DataFrame([
    subperiod_stats(bab_ts.loc[mask, "r_bab"], label)
    for mask, label in period_masks
]).set_index("Period")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bab-subperiod
#| tbl-cap: "BAB factor performance by sub-period. Ann.~Mean and Ann.~Std are annualised (multiplied by 12 and $\\sqrt{12}$). Sharpe is the ratio of annualised mean to annualised standard deviation. The $t$-statistic tests whether the mean monthly return differs from zero. $N$ is the number of months in each sub-period."
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| output: asis
_sp_display = subperiod_df[["Ann. Mean", "Ann. Std", "Sharpe", "t-stat", "N"]].copy()
_sp_display[["Ann. Mean", "Ann. Std", "Sharpe", "t-stat"]] = _sp_display[["Ann. Mean", "Ann. Std", "Sharpe", "t-stat"]].round(4)
_sp_display["N"] = _sp_display["N"].astype(int)
print(tabulate(
    _sp_display,
    headers=["", "Ann. Mean", "Ann. Std", "Sharpe", "$t$-stat", "$N$"],
    tablefmt="latex_booktabs",
    floatfmt=".4f",
    intfmt="d"
))
```

## Transaction Costs

While the gross BAB factor earns positive returns, a real-world investor must also bear the transaction costs of monthly rebalancing. To assess this, we estimate round-trip costs from daily CRSP bid-ask spreads and apply them to the turnover of each portfolio leg. The results, reported below, reveal a dramatic impact of trading frictions. Over the subsample for which transaction cost data are available, the gross BAB strategy earns an annualised mean return of 9.18% (t$=$3.94), but after deducting estimated transaction costs the net return falls to $-$51.12% per year (t$=$−13.98). The average annual transaction cost drag amounts to 60.30 percentage points, far exceeding the gross return. This implies that, under the assumption of full monthly rebalancing, the BAB strategy is entirely non-viable after accounting for realistic trading frictions. The result should be interpreted as an upper bound on actual transaction costs, since in practice investors would rebalance less frequently and only trade when the cost savings exceed the friction. Notably, the estimated annual TC drag of 60.30 percentage points exceeds even the full-sample gross BAB return of 8.85%, meaning the strategy would be non-viable under these cost assumptions regardless of which sample period is used to measure gross returns. Nonetheless, the result highlights that the gross profitability documented in section 4.2 is highly sensitive to implementation costs, particularly given the wide bid-ask spreads prevalent in CRSP data for earlier decades prior to market decimalization.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tc-results
#| tbl-cap: "Gross and net BAB returns over the transaction cost subsample (January 1993 to December 2025). Transaction costs are estimated from CRSP daily bid-ask half-spreads assuming full monthly rebalancing. Net BAB deducts the round-trip cost on both portfolio legs. Avg annual TC drag is the mean annual cost. $t$-statistics test whether the mean monthly return differs from zero."
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| output: asis
tc_display = tc_summary.round(4).copy()
print(tabulate(
    tc_display,
    headers=[""] + list(tc_display.columns),
    tablefmt="latex_booktabs",
    floatfmt=".4f",
    missingval="---"
))
```
